strengths: The paper identifies an important and under-studied failure mode: robustness work on typographic attacks can reward models for globally ignoring text, which conflicts with real LVLM use cases that require reading text in some contexts and ignoring it in others. This is a compelling benchmark motivation for ECCV.
The proposed RIO-VQA formulation is clean and useful: crossing object-vs-text questions with clean-vs-attacked images gives an intuitive way to evaluate selective text use within a shared scene.

RIO-Bench is more than a small diagnostic set. It is built from TextVQA/Open Images with explicit train/validation splits, multiple attack levels, MC and open-ended object tasks, and text-centric attacks. The authors provide construction details, dataset statistics, metrics, and examples.

The empirical coverage is broad. Results are reported for multiple LVLMs, including LLaVA, Qwen, Llama-3.2-Vision, and SmolVLM, and compare pretrained models, CoT prompting, ignore-text robust training, and the proposed balanced read-or-ignore robust training.

The main empirical finding is plausible and well supported within the constructed benchmark: object-only robust training improves object attack robustness but harms text reading, while balanced training improves the tradeoff. The paper also includes useful ablations on attack difficulty, LoRA placement, data size, attention visualizations, and some cross-dataset generalization.

The work is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution with an accompanying simple training baseline, even though no explicit contribution type is declared. Under that framing, novelty lies mainly in the benchmark/task design and diagnostic evaluation, not in the SFT method itself.
weaknesses: The benchmark quality is not sufficiently validated. The construction relies heavily on automatic Open Images labels, CLIP-based ground-truth selection, LLM-generated distractors, OCR matching heuristics, and fixed text overlays, but the paper does not report human validation of answer correctness, attack plausibility, ambiguity, or whether humans can solve the attacked text-reading cases.

Some provided examples raise concerns about data noise and ecological validity. Several attacks are rendered as small, artificial overlay text rather than scene-coherent physical text, and some examples appear semantically odd or weakly grounded. This matters because the benchmark claims to evaluate real-world selective text use under typographic attacks.

The object-VQA branch is quite template-driven. A repeated question such as “Which object is present in the image?” or “What objects can be seen in the image?” may measure shortcut behavior and label matching more than rich visual reasoning. This narrows the scope relative to the paper’s broader claims about multimodal reasoning and real-world reliability.

The open-ended object metric, R-CLIP-M, is questionable as a primary measure. It depends on CLIP text similarity, top-5 matching, and subtracting attack-word similarity, which may penalize semantically reasonable answers or reward metric artifacts. The paper would be stronger with human evaluation or a more direct parsing/classification protocol.

The training result is useful but methodologically modest: RIO-RT is essentially supervised fine-tuning on a balanced mixture of attacked object and text examples. The claim that it learns a “genuinely new capability” or “true read-or-ignore behavior” is stronger than the evidence, since models may be learning dataset-specific correlations about question templates and overlay patterns.

Generalization evidence is mixed. The external dataset table helps, but several text-centric VQA results decrease for some models, and the attacks on Typo-D/text datasets do not fully establish robustness to more realistic, adaptive, physical, or scene-coherent typographic attacks.

Important reproducibility details are promised but not yet demonstrated, such as the project page/code release. There is also a dangling “Our Project Page is at” statement in the abstract/introduction area, and the paper should clarify data licensing and release status for modified TextVQA/Open Images derivatives.

The limitations section is too brief. It acknowledges only that the scope is VQA, but should discuss artificial overlays, automatic annotation noise, English/scene-text bias, possible OCR/key-text matching failures, and whether defenses trained on the benchmark overfit to its construction process.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: LVLMs should not solve typographic robustness by globally ignoring text, because many real scenes require both object understanding and reading. The read-or-ignore framing is conceptually useful.
The benchmark design attempts controlled same-scene counterfactuals across object/text questions and clean/attack conditions, which is a reasonable direction for evaluating selective text use.
The experiments cover several LVLM families and include both inference-time and fine-tuning baselines, plus ablations on attack difficulty and LoRA placement.
weaknesses: I would assess this primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks paper with an applied training baseline, rather than an Algorithms/General paper. Under that standard, the central weakness is benchmark validity: the construction is heavily automatic, yet the paper provides little evidence that the generated questions, labels, attacks, and key-text regions are correct or unambiguous for humans.

The dataset examples raise serious quality concerns. Several appendix examples pair implausible or mismatched TextVQA questions such as “what kind of beer is this?” with scenes/answers like sports uniforms, watches, whiteboards, or numbers. This suggests the automatic one-question-per-image selection and counterfactual construction can produce semantically poor instances, directly undermining the claimed controlled evaluation.

Object-question labels are selected using Open Images annotations filtered by CLIP similarity, and open-ended evaluation uses a custom CLIP-based R-CLIP-M metric. This is a weak substitute for validated VQA labels: it may reward semantically related but incorrect answers, penalize benign mentions of attack words, and obscure whether models truly recognized the visual object.

Text-attack generation and placement rely on Llama-3 and heuristic OCR/key-text matching, but the paper does not report human validation of attack plausibility, contradiction correctness, legibility, non-occlusion, or whether the original answer remains uniquely answerable after adding distractor text.

The proposed RIO-RT defense is essentially supervised fine-tuning/data augmentation on the proposed benchmark. Its gains on RIO-Bench are therefore not surprising, and the paper overstates this as learning a new capability without sufficiently ruling out shortcut learning from the synthetic overlay distribution, font/placement artifacts, or benchmark-specific question templates.

The baselines are not strong enough to support the broad claims. The main non-training baseline is a reproduced CoT prompt, while training baselines are mostly variants of the authors’ own generated data. Simpler mixed-data baselines, prompt variants that explicitly condition on question type, OCR-aware approaches, and stronger data augmentation controls are missing.

Generalization evidence is mixed and does not fully support the claims. On external datasets, some text-centric averages decrease or improve only slightly, and the results do not establish robust selective text use beyond the synthetic RIO distribution.

The paper makes strong claims about real-world reliability, autonomous driving, and embodied AI, but the benchmark is derived from TextVQA/Open Images with simple rendered text overlays. The gap between this setup and real physical typographic attacks or safety-critical scenes is not adequately addressed.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted manuscript: the abstract leaves the project page blank, and important generation details such as prompts, filtering rates, validation procedures, random seeds, and quality-control statistics are insufficient for judging or reproducing dataset quality.

The limitations section is very narrow. It acknowledges only that the current scope is VQA, but does not seriously discuss dataset noise, synthetic text artifacts, automatic label errors, possible shortcut learning, or human ambiguity under text attacks.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: the paper identifies a real gap in typographic-attack evaluation, namely that robustness methods can appear strong by simply suppressing text reading, which is misaligned with practical vision-language use cases.

The RIO-VQA formulation is conceptually clean. Crossing object/text intent with clean/attacked conditions gives a clear way to evaluate selective text use rather than treating robustness and OCR-style reading as separate abilities.

RIO-Bench’s same-scene counterfactual design is a strong contribution for a Datasets/Benchmarks-style paper. Holding the image scene fixed while varying question type and overlaid text reduces confounding and makes failures easy to interpret.

The experimental coverage is broad: multiple LVLM families and sizes are evaluated, with comparisons among pretrained models, CoT-style prompting, ignore-text robust training, and the proposed read-or-ignore robust training.

The results support the central claim: existing models over-read misleading text, text-agnostic defenses improve object robustness while harming text-VQA, and balanced RIO-RT improves object-attack robustness while largely preserving or improving text-reading performance.

The appendix provides useful construction details, dataset statistics, attack-generation procedures, metrics, computational cost, qualitative examples, and some cross-dataset generalization evidence, which improves reproducibility and scientific value.
weaknesses: The benchmark is largely automatically constructed, and the paper does not provide enough human validation of label correctness, generated object questions, Llama-generated contradictory text, key-text localization, or whether attacked examples are genuinely answerable and unambiguous. This is important because the benchmark itself is the main contribution.

The object-centric VQA branch is somewhat narrow and templated. Multiple-choice questions use a fixed presence template, and open-ended questions rely on Open Images labels, so the benchmark may test object-label recognition more than richer visual reasoning under text distraction.

The open-ended object metric, R-CLIP-M, is plausible but not fully established. Penalizing CLIP similarity to the attack word may introduce metric artifacts, and stronger validation against human judgments or exact object-label matching would make the evaluation more convincing.

The attacks are synthetic text overlays with limited realism. Although this is controlled and useful, the benchmark may not fully capture physical or scene-coherent typographic attacks with perspective, occlusion, lighting, typography, and adversarial placement.

The defense contribution is less original than the benchmark contribution: RIO-RT is essentially supervised LoRA fine-tuning on the proposed balanced data. This is acceptable for demonstrating benchmark utility, but the paper sometimes frames it as a stronger methodological advance than warranted.

The comparison to defenses is incomplete. Some prior CLIP defenses are not adapted, and the main LVLM baseline is CoT plus a constructed IT-RT baseline. Stronger prompting, data augmentation, OCR-aware prompting, or held-out-domain robust-training baselines would better establish the advantage of RIO-RT.

There is some risk of train/evaluation coupling: RIO-RT is trained on RIO-Bench variants and evaluated heavily on the same benchmark family. The Typo-D and external text-VQA results help, but more held-out construction styles and real-world typographic examples would strengthen claims of general selective text use.
The limitations section is brief and under-discusses dataset noise, synthetic attack realism, potential benchmark gaming, and societal implications of robustness failures in deployed LVLMs.

strengths: The paper identifies a real gap in typographic-attack evaluation: existing object-centric robustness benchmarks can reward models that simply suppress all image text, which is undesirable for scene-text VQA. The proposed read-or-ignore framing is well motivated and relevant for LVLM deployment.

RIO-Bench is a thoughtful benchmark contribution. The same-scene counterfactual design, crossing object/text question intent with clean/attack conditions, is a clean way to reduce scene-level confounds and directly measure the robustness vs. text-reading trade-off.

The experimental coverage is strong for a benchmark paper: six representative LVLMs, multiple defense baselines, controlled overlay attacks, SceneTAP-style scene-coherent insertions, modern/frontier model evaluation, ablations on LoRA placement, attention visualizations, and additional transfer results on Typo-D and text-centric VQA datasets.

The paper provides useful evidence that object-only robust training and CoT-style defenses can harm text-centric performance, while balanced read-or-ignore training can improve attack robustness without the same degree of text-reading collapse. This is a clear empirical contribution even though RIO-RT itself is intentionally simple.

The benchmark construction is relatively transparent and includes a human audit with high reported validity and agreement, plus detailed appendix descriptions of question generation, attack placement, metrics, dataset statistics, and computational cost. This helps reproducibility.
weaknesses: No contribution type is explicitly declared; I assess it primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks paper rather than an Algorithms/General paper. Under that lens the benchmark and analysis are valuable, but the algorithmic novelty of RIO-RT is modest and should not be viewed as the main contribution.

The benchmark inherits limitations from TextVQA and Open Images. Object questions are mostly template-based and often ask only whether a single object class is present, while text questions come from TextVQA; this may not fully capture richer real-world situations where text and object evidence interact compositionally.

The attack construction is partly synthetic and may overrepresent visible inserted words. Although SceneTAP evaluation helps, the controlled overlay setup and LLM-generated distractors may not cover physical typography, adversarial placement strategies, multilingual text, small/low-contrast text, or dynamic/embodied settings claimed in the motivation.

The R-CLIP-M metric for open-ended object VQA is somewhat ad hoc. Subtracting attack-word retrieval can penalize multi-object answers in non-obvious ways, may yield hard-to-interpret scores, and depends on CLIP embedding behavior rather than direct semantic correctness.

The training baseline is evaluated largely on the same benchmark distribution used to define the training split. The paper includes some transfer experiments, which is good, but stronger held-out domains and unseen attack generators would be needed before concluding that RIO-RT learns broadly general read-or-ignore behavior.

The human audit covers only 400 samples out of a much larger automatically generated benchmark. The reported rates are reassuring, but more stratified auditing by difficulty level, attack type, model failure category, and text-key matching fallback cases would strengthen confidence in benchmark quality.

Some claims are phrased broadly, such as exposing a fundamental misalignment with real-world multimodal requirements. The evidence supports a meaningful benchmark-level misalignment, but the real-world deployment implications remain only partially validated.

strengths: The paper identifies a real blind spot in typographic-attack evaluation: object-centric robustness can be achieved by suppressing all text sensitivity, which is undesirable for LVLMs that must also read scene text. Framing this as a read-or-ignore VQA problem is useful and relevant to computer vision deployment settings.

RIO-Bench has a clear counterfactual design: object/text question intent crossed with clean/attack text conditions on the same base scenes. This is a sensible benchmark contribution, especially because it makes the robustness/text-reading trade-off directly measurable.

The empirical coverage is broad: multiple LVLM families, multiple model scales, open-source and closed-source models, controlled overlays and SceneTAP-style insertions, plus transfer checks to Typo-D and other text-centric VQA datasets.

The paper includes reasonable validation steps, including a human audit of generated examples, analysis of attack difficulty, LoRA placement ablations, qualitative examples, and limitations. This makes the experimental story more complete than a simple benchmark release.

The RIO-RT baseline is simple but effective as a reference point: balanced training on read and ignore cases consistently improves attacked object performance while avoiding the severe text-reading degradation seen in the ignore-text training baseline.
weaknesses: The main conceptual contribution is somewhat incremental: the paper repackages a natural desideratum for LVLMs, namely use question context to decide whether text is relevant, into a benchmark. The novelty is more in benchmark organization than in a new technical method or deep analysis of the underlying mechanism.

The claimed same-scene counterfactual control is imperfect. Object questions are derived from Open Images labels and CLIP scoring rather than human-authored object VQA annotations, so the selected object may not always be salient or visually unambiguous. This weakens the premise that only question intent and text condition vary while all other factors are controlled.

The object open-ended metric, R-CLIP-M, is ad hoc and may be hard to interpret. Subtracting an attack-word retrieval score from a CLIP-based semantic match can penalize partially correct answers in unclear ways and depends strongly on the label vocabulary and CLIP embedding behavior rather than direct answer correctness.

The attack generation process may introduce ambiguity, especially for Text-Attack cases where LLM-generated contradictory text is inserted into images that already contain relevant text. The human audit covers only 400 samples out of a much larger benchmark, so the evidence for benchmark validity is helpful but not fully convincing.

The defense comparison is not entirely satisfying. IT-RT is intentionally trained only on object-attack data, while RIO-RT receives balanced object and text attack supervision; the observed trade-off is therefore partly built into the training setup. This supports the benchmark’s diagnosis but is less compelling as evidence of a superior defense principle.

The paper sometimes overstates its conclusions. Terms such as “fundamental misalignment” are stronger than what the experiments establish, since the study is scoped to TextVQA-derived images, synthetic/edited inserted text, VQA-style prompting, and a limited set of defenses.

Reproducibility depends on several generated components: Llama-generated attack words, CLIP-based object selection, OCR/key-text matching, SceneTAP/GPT-4o-based placement, and diffusion insertion. The paper gives useful details but the benchmark’s exact recreation may still be brittle unless the dataset, generated artifacts, and evaluation scripts are fully released.

The practical impact is plausible but not yet demonstrated in realistic downstream settings such as navigation, driving, or embodied decision-making. The paper motivates these applications, but evaluation remains mostly within benchmark-style VQA.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and under-evaluated failure mode: typographic robustness methods can appear successful by suppressing text sensitivity, which is undesirable for LVLMs that must also read scene text. The read-or-ignore framing is clear, timely, and well motivated for computer vision applications involving multimodal perception.

RIO-Bench is a well designed benchmark contribution. The same-scene counterfactual structure, crossing object/text question intent with clean/attack conditions, is a strong way to reduce scene-level confounds and directly measure selective text use.

The construction is reasonably careful: it leverages TextVQA and Open Images dual annotations, avoids occluding OCR text, includes both controlled overlay attacks and SceneTAP-style scene-coherent insertions, and provides train/evaluation splits with multiple difficulty levels and question formats.

The experimental evidence is broad and useful. The paper evaluates several LVLM families and sizes, multiple defense settings, modern/frontier models, attack difficulty, LoRA placement, external datasets, and qualitative attention visualizations. The main trend is consistent: object-centric defenses often hurt text-centric performance, while balanced read-or-ignore training mitigates this trade-off.

The human audit and inter-annotator agreement analysis strengthen the benchmark validity, and the limitations section appropriately acknowledges that the work is scoped to LVLM VQA and does not exhaust real-world typography or adversarial threat models.
weaknesses: The main defense, RIO-RT, is intentionally simple and its gains are somewhat expected because it is trained directly on the benchmark’s read/ignore construction. This is acceptable for a benchmark paper, but it limits the algorithmic novelty and makes the defense more of a reference baseline than a substantive method contribution.

RIO-Bench inherits important scope limitations from TextVQA/Open Images. The object-centric questions are largely template-based and label-driven, while the text branch is tied to one scene-text VQA source. This may not fully capture richer real-world reasoning where text, objects, layout, and actions interact more naturally.

The object-VQA open-ended evaluation relies on R-CLIP-M, which is useful but nonstandard and potentially sensitive to CLIP embedding behavior, synonym handling, and the subtraction term for attack-word retrieval. More validation of this metric against human judgments or alternative scoring would make the benchmark stronger.

The human audit covers only 400 samples relative to the benchmark size, and the review would benefit from more detail on sampling, failure categories, and whether quality varies by attack type, difficulty level, or question format.

The baseline comparison is somewhat uneven: RIO-RT and IT-RT are fine-tuned methods, while CoT is an inference-time prompt defense, and several prior CLIP defenses are excluded or only adapted conceptually. The paper explains this constraint, but stronger or more diverse LVLM-specific baselines would make the empirical claims more convincing.

The attacks are still mostly synthetic or generated insertions. SceneTAP improves realism, but the benchmark does not establish robustness under physical-world typography, natural sign clutter, multilingual text, handwritten text, or adversarial placements optimized against particular models. These limits matter given the real-world motivation.
